extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, caption-writers, and entrants to The New Yorker Caption Contest; humor writers aiming for New Yorker-style cartoons
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for writing and selecting single-panel cartoon captions in the New Yorker register, including what makes a caption suitable for publication or as a Caption Contest winner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise is essential / Genuine surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise is the essential ingredient in humor. Surprise violates expectations; when the unexpected occurs and we realize there's nothing to worry about, we laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong caption should produce a genuine element of surprise. Avoid predictable punchlines and warmed-over jokes. The surprise should resolve cleanly rather than relying on shock alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscenity, aggression, cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: What New Yorker cartoons AVOID — obscenity, aggression, cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Yorker intentionally removes these levers of humor. Anti-patterns include crude sexual language, gratuitous violence, or mean-spirited cruelty. Tone should be urbane rather than hostile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original premise (no warmed-over situations)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fresh, specific scenarios over clichés or recycled setups. Originality of premise increases perceived cleverness even if the mechanism is familiar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific drawing (use of distinctive visual detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific drawing (Roz Chast's wallpaper, Charles Addams's gloom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good captions exploit particular, identifiable features of the artwork rather than generic descriptions. Reference to concrete visual details makes the caption feel tailored to the cartoon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption fits the drawing exactly — not interchangeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Caption fits the drawing exactly — not interchangeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong caption should be inseparable from the artwork; if the same caption could work on many drawings, it's weaker. Aim for specificity that ties wording to the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle, not over-explained
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid spelling out the joke or belaboring the setup. Let the reader make the connection; over-explanation reduces wit and undermines the payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twoness — drawing and caption say different things that resolve
rubrics_metrics.description: "Twoness" — drawing says one thing, caption another, both resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most satisfying cartoons create a productive tension between visual and verbal elements; the caption should reframe or contradict the drawing in a way that resolves into humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wry/urbane register (the "New Yorker-y" voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Winner is most "New Yorker-y" — wry, urbane, character-mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone should be urbane, understated, and character-focused rather than broad or slapstick. Phrasing, diction, and point-of-view should feel consistent with New Yorker sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could the caption become quotable / reusable
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the caption become quotable / reusable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captions that function as memorable one-liners or conversational quotes have extra value. Reusability and quotability signal broad resonance beyond the panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversational tone (as in "How about never—is never good for you?").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A natural, offhand conversational voice often heightens relatability and comedic effect. Avoid overly staged or theatrical phrasing when a casual tone would serve better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness mask / Devastating refusal as a technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Politeness mask — politeness conceals a devastating refusal (e.g., "How about never—is never good for you?").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using polite or understated language to deliver a blunt or cutting idea magnifies comic contrast. This technique should be used with subtlety rather than sarcasm for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection workflow and triage (keepers / maybe / no)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caption Contest Selection Insights — Mankoff and team examine ~5,000 captions per week and sort them into three buckets: keepers, maybe, no; keepers are re-read and finalists chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the editorial process: many submissions are filtered quickly; to reach 'keepers' a caption must stand out on first read and survive subsequent re-reads. Finalists are judged for 'New Yorker-y' qualities.
